title: A map of n-coskeletal simplicial sets, bijective below n and surjective in degree n, is a trivial Kan fibration
statement: Let $f:V\to U$ be a morphism of simplicial sets [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set] and $n\geq0$. Assume (1) $f_i:V_i\to U_i$ is bijective for $i<n$; (2) $f_n:V_n\to U_n$ is surjective; (3) the canonical morphism $U\to\operatorname{cosk}_n\mathrm{sk}_nU$ [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-coskeleton] is an isomorphism; (4) the canonical morphism $V\to\operatorname{cosk}_n\mathrm{sk}_nV$ is an isomorphism. Then $f$ is a trivial Kan fibration [def-weil-pbc-trivial-kan-fibration].

proof.text: Notation. By [def-weil-pbc-trivial-kan-fibration] we must show (a) $f_0:V_0\to U_0$ is surjective and (b) for every $k\geq1$ and morphisms $a:\partial\Delta[k]\to V$, $b:\Delta[k]\to U$ with $f\circ a=b\circ\iota$, where $\iota:\partial\Delta[k]\to\Delta[k]$ is the inclusion, there is $c:\Delta[k]\to V$ with $c\circ\iota=a$ and $f\circ c=b$. For (a): if $n=0$, $f_0$ is surjective by (2); if $n\geq1$, then $0<n$ and $f_0$ is bijective by (1).

source.place: Simplicial, Lemma 01A6 (lemma-section), proof: 'Consider a solid diagram ... as in Definition 08NL'

proof.text: Case $1\leq k\leq n$. Put $x=b_k(\mathrm{id}_{[k]})\in U_k$; by naturality of $b$, $b_m(\varphi)=b_m(\Delta[k](\varphi)(\mathrm{id}_{[k]}))=U(\varphi)(x)$ for every $\varphi:[m]\to[k]$. By (1) (if $k<n$) or (2) (if $k=n$) choose $y\in V_k$ with $f_k(y)=x$, and define $c_m(\varphi)=V(\varphi)(y)$ for $\varphi\in\Delta[k]_m$; since $V(\varphi\circ\psi)=V(\psi)\circ V(\varphi)$, $c:\Delta[k]\to V$ is a morphism of simplicial sets. Then $f_m(c_m(\varphi))=f_m(V(\varphi)(y))=U(\varphi)(f_k(y))=U(\varphi)(x)=b_m(\varphi)$, so $f\circ c=b$. For $c\circ\iota=a$, let $\varphi:[m]\to[k]$ be non-surjective, choose $i\in[k]$ outside its image and write $\varphi=\delta_i\circ\psi$ with $\psi:[m]\to[k-1]$ by [lem-weil-pbc-simplex-face-factorization]. Since $\delta_i\in\partial\Delta[k]_{k-1}$ and $a$ is natural, $a_m(\varphi)=V(\psi)(a_{k-1}(\delta_i))$, while $c_m(\varphi)=V(\psi)(V(\delta_i)(y))$. So it suffices that $a_{k-1}(\delta_i)=V(\delta_i)(y)$ in $V_{k-1}$. Both have the same image under $f_{k-1}$: $f_{k-1}(a_{k-1}(\delta_i))=b_{k-1}(\delta_i)=U(\delta_i)(x)=U(\delta_i)(f_k(y))=f_{k-1}(V(\delta_i)(y))$. As $k-1<n$, $f_{k-1}$ is injective by (1), so they are equal. (This is the source's 'the diagram will commute as the other nondegenerate simplices of $\Delta[k]$ are in degrees $<k$ where $f$ is an isomorphism'.)

source.place: Simplicial, Lemma 01A6 (lemma-section), proof: 'If $k\leq n$ then the dotted arrow is the one corresponding to a lift $y\in V_k$ of $x$ ...'

proof.text: Maps into an $n$-coskeletal simplicial set. Let $W$ be a simplicial set such that the canonical morphism $\gamma:W\to C=\operatorname{cosk}_n\mathrm{sk}_nW$, with counit $\varepsilon:\mathrm{sk}_nC\to\mathrm{sk}_nW$, is an isomorphism [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-coskeleton]. Then for every simplicial set $K$ the map $\Theta_K:g\mapsto\mathrm{sk}_n(g)$, $\operatorname{Mor}(K,W)\to\operatorname{Mor}(\mathrm{sk}_nK,\mathrm{sk}_nW)$, is bijective. Indeed, by definition of the canonical morphism, $\varepsilon\circ\mathrm{sk}_n(\gamma)=\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{sk}_nW}$; by definition of the coskeleton, $h\mapsto\varepsilon\circ\mathrm{sk}_n(h)$ is a bijection $\operatorname{Mor}(K,C)\to\operatorname{Mor}(\mathrm{sk}_nK,\mathrm{sk}_nW)$; and $g\mapsto\gamma\circ g$ is a bijection $\operatorname{Mor}(K,W)\to\operatorname{Mor}(K,C)$ since $\gamma$ is an isomorphism. The composite is $g\mapsto\varepsilon\circ\mathrm{sk}_n(\gamma)\circ\mathrm{sk}_n(g)=\mathrm{sk}_n(g)$, using that $\mathrm{sk}_n$ is a functor. By (3) and (4) this applies to $W=U$ and $W=V$.

source.place: Simplicial, Lemma 01A6 (lemma-section), proof: 'by conditions (3) and (4) we have (using adjointness of skeleton and coskeleton functors) $\mathrm{Mor}(\Delta[k],U)=\mathrm{Mor}(\mathrm{sk}_n\Delta[k],\mathrm{sk}_nU)$'

proof.text: For $k>n$ the morphism $\mathrm{sk}_n(\iota):\mathrm{sk}_n\partial\Delta[k]\to\mathrm{sk}_n\Delta[k]$ is an isomorphism (indeed the identity): for $j\leq n<k$ no order-preserving map $[j]\to[k]$ is surjective (its image has at most $j+1<k+1$ elements), so $\partial\Delta[k]_j=\Delta[k]_j$ and $\iota_j$ is the identity for all $j\leq n$.

Hence for $k>n$ and $W\in\{U,V\}$ the restriction $r_W:\operatorname{Mor}(\Delta[k],W)\to\operatorname{Mor}(\partial\Delta[k],W)$, $g\mapsto g\circ\iota$, is bijective: by functoriality $\Theta_{\partial\Delta[k]}(g\circ\iota)=\Theta_{\Delta[k]}(g)\circ\mathrm{sk}_n(\iota)$, so $r_W=\Theta_{\partial\Delta[k]}^{-1}\circ(-\circ\mathrm{sk}_n(\iota))\circ\Theta_{\Delta[k]}$ is a composite of three bijections (step 3 twice, and precomposition with the isomorphism of step 4).

source.place: Simplicial, Lemma 01A6 (lemma-section), proof: '$\mathrm{Mor}(\Delta[k],U)=\mathrm{Mor}(\mathrm{sk}_n\Delta[k],\mathrm{sk}_nU)=\mathrm{Mor}(\mathrm{sk}_n\partial\Delta[k],\mathrm{sk}_nU)=\mathrm{Mor}(\partial\Delta[k],U)$ and similarly for $V$'

proof.text: Case $k>n$ (this includes $k=n+1$). Given $a,b$ as in step 1, let $c=r_V^{-1}(a):\Delta[k]\to V$, so $c\circ\iota=a$. Then $r_U(f\circ c)=f\circ c\circ\iota=f\circ a=b\circ\iota=r_U(b)$, and injectivity of $r_U$ (step 5) gives $f\circ c=b$. Together with step 2 (for $1\leq k\leq n$) and step 1 (a), $f$ is a trivial Kan fibration [def-weil-pbc-trivial-kan-fibration]; for $k>n$ the lift is moreover unique.
